groups.d: Science-look views that tell you what is in the sound, not just draw it.
Shaping a track from start to finish, with the energy visible.
Tools that show where the problem is and leave the decision to you.
Learning inside your own project instead of in a video.
Builds on the Time Machine AudioLab already has.
Keeping the good moments you did not plan to record.

groups.n: AI that helps without taking over
groups.d: Suggestions you can see, compare, accept one by one and undo.
Hearing and feeling what the screen shows.

ideas.t: Frequency map of the whole song
ideas.sees: One wide picture of the full song: time left to right, frequency bottom to top (log, 20 Hz to 20 kHz), each pixel coloured by the track that owns the most energy there. Section names from the arrangement sit along the top. Click any spot: the arrangement jumps there and that track is selected. A switch shows a single track as a glowing layer over the rest.
ideas.why: Answers "what is happening where" for a whole psytrance track in one look: whether the sub is owned by one track, where the leads and the pads pile up at 2 to 5 kHz, which section is thin. A normal spectrum shows only the present moment and mixes all tracks together.
ideas.prior: Spectrograms exist everywhere (Sonic Visualiser layers, iZotope RX); iZotope Neutron's masking meter compares two tracks at a time inside a plug-in. A whole-song, per-track ownership map inside the DAW was not found.
ideas.risks: Needs an offline analysis pass of every track (cost grows with track count; do it in a worker, cache per clip). Colours for 30 tracks need grouping by the track colours or by bus.
ideas.effort: 2 tasks (analysis worker and cache; the map view and click-to-jump)
ideas.native: No. Works with the web engine's offline render; the native engine later makes the pass faster.

ideas.sees: A note ruler (C0 to C3) with the song key's notes lit. The kick's pitch is drawn as its falling curve over its 300 ms life, with the note it settles on marked. The bass notes of the current bar are bars on the same ruler. Where the kick tail and a bass note sit a semitone or two apart, the gap glows red and the beat rate is shown ("beating at 3.4 Hz"). Buttons: tune the kick to the key root, or shift the bass by an octave. For rolling psytrance bass, a strip shows the gap the bass leaves for each kick.
ideas.why: Kick-bass clashes are the classic low-end problem in psytrance and EDM. Producers tune kicks by ear with a tuner device and a note chart. Seeing both on one pitch ruler in the song's key turns a guessing job into a reading.
ideas.prior: Kick plug-ins (for example Sonic Academy Kick) show the kick's pitch envelope; tuners show one note; tutorials teach tuning by ear and nudging the bass 1 to 5 ms (MusicRadar). Nothing found that draws kick and bass on one ruler with the key.
ideas.risks: Pitch tracking of a kick's short tail is not exact under 40 Hz; show it as a range. Psytrance kicks often do not settle on a clean note.
ideas.effort: 2 tasks (pitch track of kick samples and synth kick; the view and the two fixes)

ideas.sees: Click a red clip light on the master or on any strip. A card opens with the moment it happened (bar and beat) and a short chain: "Kick + Bass add up here: +2.1 dB over 0 dBFS. Biggest share: Bass (58%), Kick (31%). Inter-sample peak: +0.6 dB." Each line has a fix button: lower the bass by 5 dB, turn on the limiter, play the moment again. A small bar chart shows each track's share of the peak.
ideas.why: Every DAW shows THAT something clipped, none says WHY. Beginners lower the master fader, which fixes nothing upstream. Tracing the peak back to the tracks that made it is exactly the "smart and sciencey" help the app is aiming for.
ideas.prior: Clip indicators and peak-hold everywhere; loudness meters with history. A causal breakdown by track was not found.
ideas.risks: A peak is a sum of signals with phase, so "share" needs a careful definition (contribution at the peak sample, signed). Needs short per-track ring buffers around each clip event.
ideas.native: No. The ring buffers are cheaper in the native engine later.

ideas.sees: Next to the existing Mono check: a band-by-band bar per track showing how much level that track loses when the mix is folded to mono ("Pad: −7 dB at 200 to 800 Hz"). Tracks that cancel each other are joined by a line.
ideas.why: Mono check tells you the mix sounds worse in mono; it does not tell you which track and which band. Club systems and phones are mono in the low end.
ideas.prior: Correlation meters and per-band imagers exist as plug-ins (for example in mastering suites). Per-track, per-band loss inside the mixer was not found.
ideas.risks: Needs a mid and side analysis per track; cheap with existing analysers but many tracks add up.

ideas.sees: Any spectrum view can show a piano strip under it. Peaks are labelled with their note and cents ("A1 −12 c"); peaks outside the song's scale glow amber, resonances that ring longer than a beat glow red.
ideas.why: Turns a spectrum from a picture into a reading in musical terms: a resonance becomes "that F# rings". Helps tuning, EQ and finding a bad note in a pad.
ideas.prior: Some analysers show the note under the mouse (for example Voxengo SPAN, not verified). Scale-aware labelling of all peaks was not found.
ideas.risks: Busy at full mix; show only the five strongest peaks.

ideas.sees: A thin curve under the arrangement: loudness, density (how many tracks play) and brightness over the song, with the sections marked. A dashed curve can show a reference track's arc or a typical psytrance arc (build, drop, break, second drop).
ideas.why: You see the shape of the song: whether the drop really lifts, whether the break is long enough, whether the second half sags. DJs read this kind of energy curve; producers rarely get it inside their DAW.
ideas.prior: DJ software analyses phrases and energy (rekordbox phrase analysis, Mixed In Key energy level). In a DAW arrangement: not found.
ideas.risks: "Energy" is a made-up measure; keep the three ingredients visible so it can be trusted.

ideas.sees: Draw the energy curve you want with the mouse above the arrangement. The app marks where the song falls short ("bars 97 to 112 sit 4 dB under your line") and offers moves you can try one at a time: a riser, a filter sweep, a drum fill, a layer to add. Nothing is changed until you click.
ideas.why: Starts from the musical intention (where should it build) instead of from tools. Fits the user's way of working on long psytrance structures.
ideas.prior: None found. Research on generative arrangement exists, but not this kind of target curve in a DAW.
ideas.risks: Suggestions can feel generic; they must come from your own project (your sounds, your automation). Builds on I6.

ideas.sees: Right-click a MIDI clip: "Breed variations". Six children appear as a small tree, each a mutation (notes moved, rhythm shifted, octave jumps) at a strength you set. Play them, pick one, breed again from it, or cross two clips. The tree stays with the clip so you can go back to any ancestor.
ideas.why: Sound design by choosing instead of by programming: you only judge with your ears. Good for acid lines and psytrance bass patterns where small changes matter. The tree looks like a phylogenetic chart, which fits the science look.
ideas.prior: Sonic Charge Synplant breeds synth patches; genetic-algorithm music research (for example Biles' GenJam). For clips inside a DAW, with a kept tree: not found.
ideas.risks: Random mutations can be boring; mutations must respect the scale lock and the groove.

ideas.sees: Select the border between two sections. Three or four transitions are prepared and can be played in place: riser plus filter sweep, reverse crash and snare roll, a one-bar cut to silence, a tape stop. Pick one: it is built from AudioLab's own devices on its own track, editable.
ideas.why: Transitions are where tracks lose momentum, and making them is repetitive. Hearing options in context beats dragging samples around.
ideas.prior: Sample packs of transitions; some apps offer riser generators. Context-aware options built at the section border: not found.
ideas.risks: Can make every song sound the same; options should use the song's own sounds where possible.

ideas.sees: Drop a finished reference track on a ghost lane above the arrangement. Its sections are found and lined up with yours (drop to drop). While playing, a split meter compares the matching sections: loudness, low end, width.
ideas.why: Comparing "my drop" with "their drop" at the right moment, without jumping around.
ideas.prior: Reference plug-ins (for example Mastering The Mix REFERENCE, ADPTR Metric AB) compare level-matched audio, not section by section against your arrangement.
ideas.risks: Section finding in someone else's track is a guess; let the user drag the boundaries.

ideas.sees: While the song plays, whatever is changing the sound right now glows softly: the automation lane, the LFO, the knob being moved by it, the cable from the modulator. Pause and the glow freezes, so you can see what was moving at that moment.
ideas.why: "Where is that wobble coming from?" is a common hunt in big projects. Strudel lights up the exact piece of code that is playing; this does the same for devices.
ideas.prior: Strudel's live highlighting of the playing code ("temporal source mapping"); Bitwig shows modulation amounts on knobs. A song-wide glow of everything that is moving: not found.
ideas.risks: Visual noise in busy songs; a filter for "only the selected track" is needed. Glass and frame-rate budget.

ideas.sees: With "Clashes" on, the mixer's cable lane shows a cable between two strips that fight in a band right now, its thickness the size of the overlap, labelled with the band ("Bass vs Kick, 45 to 70 Hz"). Click the cable: options to duck one under the other in that band only, or to carve a little EQ notch.
ideas.why: Masking is the hardest mix problem to hear. AudioLab's cable system is the part the user loves, so showing clashes as cables reuses a picture the user already reads well.
ideas.prior: iZotope Neutron's masking meter (one pair, inside a plug-in, "does not fix them automatically", Sound On Sound). Across the whole mixer, with cables: not found.
ideas.risks: Pairwise comparison grows with the square of track count; limit to the 12 loudest tracks or to the selected track. Must not clutter the cable lane: its own colour and a switch.

ideas.sees: For one channel, a vertical strip that follows the signal from the clip through each device to the fader and the bus: level in and out at every step as a small waterfall, with the biggest jumps marked.
ideas.why: Gain staging is invisible: each device has its own meter, if any. One picture of the whole path shows where the level jumps or drops.
ideas.prior: Per-plug-in meters; some channel strips show input and output. A whole-path view: not found.
ideas.risks: Needs a tap after every device; cheap with analysers, but only for the selected channel.

ideas.sees: When you compare two versions (Mix A/B, two EQ settings, two kicks), a "Blind" button hides which is which, level-matches them and plays them in random order. You vote; after five rounds it shows whether you really heard a difference.
ideas.why: A louder version always sounds better. Blind, level-matched comparison is how engineers stop fooling themselves, and AudioLab already has Mix A/B to build on.
ideas.prior: ABX test tools for audio formats; level matching in some reference plug-ins. Inside a DAW's own A/B: not found.
ideas.risks: Some users will find it a gimmick; keep it one button.

ideas.sees: A row of small lenses on the master: phone speaker, laptop, earbuds, car, club PA (big low end, mono below 120 Hz), and "sub only". One click hears the mix through it.
ideas.why: Mixes are checked on many systems; walking to the car is slow. Ties in with the DAC and audiophile work in Settings.
ideas.prior: Plug-ins exist (for example Audified MixChecker, Sonarworks). Built into the master section of a DAW: rare. Close to RF1's field; kept here because the club PA and sub-only lenses are tuned for psytrance.
ideas.risks: Simulations are approximations; label them as such. Must be off for export.

ideas.sees: A small dose meter near the loudness read-out: how much sound your ears have had in this session (level times time, from the output level and the DAC setting). After a long loud stretch it suggests a break; after a break, "fresh ears" plays your mix and a reference for 20 seconds before you change anything.
ideas.why: Mixing decisions made with tired ears are the ones you undo the next day. AudioLab already has a headphone safety ceiling; this adds the time dimension.
ideas.prior: Phone and watch headphone-exposure tracking. In a DAW: not found.
ideas.risks: The real level at the ear is unknown without calibration; show it as an estimate and let the user calibrate once. Not medical advice.

ideas.t: Explain mode with a live picture
ideas.sees: Hold a key and hover any knob: a small card explains it in one line and shows a live picture of what it does to the sound you are playing (attack reshapes the drawn envelope, the filter cutoff moves on a mini spectrum).
ideas.why: Learning by seeing the effect on your own sound, not on a textbook example. Ableton's Info View explains in text only.
ideas.prior: Ableton Info View (text). Live pictures per control: not found.
ideas.risks: Needs a picture type for each kind of control; start with filter, envelope, compressor and delay.

ideas.t: Recipe cards that act on your project
ideas.sees: A card like "Rolling psytrance bass in 6 steps". Each step points at the real control in your project (it glows), says what to listen for, and ticks itself when the change is made. Cards can be written as extension files (docs/extensions-plan.md).
ideas.why: Tutorials live in videos, away from the work. Here the steps happen in your own song.
ideas.prior: Ableton's built-in lessons and the Learning Music site (outside your project). Steps that watch your real project: not found.
ideas.risks: Writing good cards takes time; start with four for the user's genres.

ideas.t: Ear training on your own mix
ideas.sees: A two-minute game: AudioLab boosts a band on one of your tracks and you guess the frequency, or it changes a compressor and you guess which one. Score and progress are kept.
ideas.why: Training on your own sounds transfers better to your own mixing than training on generic loops.
ideas.prior: Ear-training apps such as SoundGym and TrainYourEars (separate apps with their own audio). Inside a DAW with your audio: not found.
ideas.risks: Fun is hard to design; keep it short and optional.

ideas.sees: All 1,238 presets as a star map: similar sounds sit close together, colour by instrument, brightness by how bright the sound is. Hover to hear, drag a lasso to collect favourites, type "dark pluck" to light up a region.
ideas.why: Browsing by sound instead of by name. The star map fits the Webb and Hubble look of the app.
ideas.prior: XLN Audio XO arranges drum samples as a map; Sononym maps samples. For synth presets of a DAW's own instruments: not found.
ideas.risks: Needs one render and analysis per preset (offline, once).

ideas.sees: Once a month, a private one-page report from your own projects: "You boost 3 to 4 kHz on leads in 80% of songs", "your sub sits 2 dB above your references", "you finish songs in about 9 sessions".
ideas.why: Habits are invisible from the inside. Seeing your own tendencies is how you improve without a teacher.
ideas.prior: Not found.
ideas.risks: Can feel like being watched; local only, opt in, easy to delete.

ideas.sees: The Time Machine's timeline gets a scrub bar: drag it and hear the same 8 bars as they sounded in each saved version, like a time-lapse of the song growing. Two versions can be put side by side for a quick A/B, and one track can be pulled out of an old version into today's song.
ideas.why: "It sounded better on Tuesday" can be checked in seconds instead of opening old files. Pulling one track from the past fixes the case where only one part got worse.
ideas.prior: Endlesss keeps every jam step as a playable rifff ("go back in the timeline and keep working from there"); game replays and Braid-style time rewind. In a DAW's version history: not found.
ideas.risks: Each version needs a short render, cached in the background; storage grows (needs the storage read-out the settings audit asked for).

ideas.sees: Select tracks or a time range, then "Undo here": steps back only the changes that touched that selection and leaves the rest of your later work alone. The undo history list highlights which steps that will be.
ideas.why: Today, undoing a mistake made an hour ago on the bass also undoes everything done since on the drums.
ideas.prior: Emacs undo-tree's "undo in region" (records a new branch, never edits history). In a DAW: not found.
ideas.risks: Changes that depend on each other (a moved clip that was later edited) need clear rules; refuse with a reason when a step cannot be separated.

ideas.sees: A "Try" button in the top bar. Press it and everything from now on happens on a side branch, shown by a coloured outline around the app and a branch name. At any time: Keep (merge into the song), Drop (back to before, nothing lost), or Keep both (the branch becomes a version in the Time Machine). Branches can be compared with Mix A/B.
ideas.why: Fear of breaking a good mix stops people from experimenting. Making the experiment explicit and free removes that fear. The Time Machine already has a version tree, so branches have a home.
ideas.prior: Git branches; Emacs undo-tree; Endlesss' forward-only rifffs. In a DAW as one button: not found.
ideas.risks: Merging is only simple if the branch replaces the song (no three-way merge); say so. Audio recorded on a branch needs its files kept until the branch is dropped.

ideas.sees: When you open a project, a short card: "Last time (Tuesday, 2 h): you built the second drop, added the Growl lead, left the break unfinished", with an 8-bar sound snapshot of where you stopped. Write a note to your future self on closing.
ideas.why: Getting back into a song after days away is a real cost. The diary is made from the undo history, so it costs you nothing.
ideas.prior: Not found in DAWs.
ideas.risks: Summaries from undo steps can be dull; keep them to three lines, optionally written by the Assistant.

ideas.sees: Right-click any knob: a small timeline of its last values in this session. Drag along it to scrub the knob back in time while hearing it, then let go to keep that value.
ideas.why: "It sounded better a minute ago" for a single control, without undoing everything else. Like rewinding time in a game.
ideas.prior: Braid-style rewind in games. In a DAW: not found.
ideas.risks: Memory per parameter must be small (ring buffer of values, not audio).

ideas.t: Capture knob moves after the fact
ideas.sees: AudioLab's Capture already keeps the notes you played. This keeps knob and fader moves too: after a great filter sweep you did while jamming, press Capture and it becomes automation at the right place.
ideas.why: The best moves happen when you are not recording.
ideas.prior: Ableton's Capture MIDI and Endlesss' retrospective looper capture notes and audio; for automation: not found.
ideas.risks: Needs a ring buffer of control changes; cheap.

ideas.sees: Save up to four snapshots of chosen knobs (for example two filter and delay settings). An XY pad morphs smoothly between them, and the path you draw can be recorded as automation.
ideas.why: One gesture for a big change, useful for live sets and for long psytrance builds.
ideas.prior: Elektron Octatrack scenes and crossfader; some plug-ins morph presets. As a DAW-wide pad over any knob: rare.
ideas.risks: Close to features in other tools; RF1 may list it too.

ideas.sees: In a live or loop view, a ring around the play button fills over the current 8 or 16-bar phrase. Launched clips wait for the next phrase and show a countdown in beats.
ideas.why: Psytrance and EDM are built in 8 and 16-bar phrases; launching at the phrase keeps a live set clean.
ideas.prior: Launch quantisation in clip-based DAWs; phrase analysis in DJ software. The phrase ring itself: not found.
ideas.risks: Small; mostly visual.

ideas.sees: Whatever the Assistant proposes appears as ghosts, never as changes: ghost notes in the piano roll, a ghost automation line, a ghost EQ curve over the real one. Each ghost has a tick and a cross; "Hear it" plays the song with the ghost included. Accepted ghosts are marked as AI-made in the undo history.
ideas.why: Surveys agree: musicians accept AI for help and reject AI that decides. 93% prefer more control even if slower, 43% want changes labelled, 39% want undo and compare (Muse Group, 2026). Ghosts are control, labels and compare in one picture.
ideas.prior: Ghost notes from other clips exist in AudioLab and other DAWs; AI tools usually apply their changes directly (Neutron's Mix Assistant moves Relay faders). Every AI change as an acceptable ghost: not found.
ideas.risks: Each kind of change needs its own ghost drawing; start with notes and automation. Plays well with the extensions plan (stage 4 tools).

ideas.sees: Ask the Assistant a question about the song: "Why does the second drop feel weaker?" It answers with measurements, not opinions ("the second drop is 1.8 dB quieter, 30% narrower, and the lead is missing between bars 161 and 176"), each with a link that jumps there.
ideas.why: An answer you can check is one you can trust. Uses the same measurements as I1, I3 and I6.
ideas.prior: Chat assistants in DAWs mostly do actions or general advice. Answers grounded in measurements of your own project: not found.
ideas.risks: Needs a model connection for free questions; without one, a set of fixed questions works offline.

ideas.t: Fill the gap from your own clips
ideas.sees: Select an empty bar or two: the Assistant offers fills made only from material in this song (variations of your own clips, in key and tempo), as ghosts (I30).
ideas.why: The study of producers using text-to-music tools found wrong tempo and key, no editing and no partial regeneration were the main problems (Ronchini et al., 2025). Working from your own clips avoids all three and the training-data worry.
ideas.prior: Generative MIDI tools (in other DAWs and plug-ins) use their own models; RF1 covers those. Restricting to the song's own material: rare.
ideas.risks: Variety is limited to what is in the song; that is the point.

ideas.sees: A switch that tints everything the AI made or changed (notes, automation, stems, device settings). A read-out "AI share of this song: 6% of notes, 2 stems". One button removes all AI changes, and the export can include a short honest credit line.
ideas.why: Only 6% of creators would hide AI use, and most want clear labelling (Sound On Sound 2026 survey; Muse Group). Knowing where the AI was keeps authorship clear.
ideas.prior: Not found in DAWs.
ideas.risks: Every AI tool must tag its changes; easy if done from the start (stage 4 of the extensions plan).

ideas.sees: For anyone who cannot or does not want to look: levels as a soft pitch in one ear, a short earcon when a track clips or the master passes the loudness target, and "Describe the mix" which reads a short summary ("Bass loudest, master −8 LUFS, two tracks clip in the drop"). Haptics on supported trackpads and controllers.
ideas.why: "The majority of commercially available DAWs are not designed to be compatible with screen readers" (Karpodini et al.). Blind producers rely on REAPER with the OSARA add-on; building it in is rare. Earcons also help sighted users mixing with eyes closed.
ideas.prior: OSARA for REAPER (screen reader support, peak reports); research on haptic meters (Karpodini et al., BCU). Built into a DAW: rare.
ideas.risks: Needs testing with screen reader users; sighted design guesses go wrong.
ideas.native: No (haptics on Mac trackpads need the native app).
